metadata.title: Patterns and Pixelation
metadata.audience: people making games in Godot, and anyone directing an AI that writes shaders for them
metadata.lecture_opening_description: How cells make blocks, checkers, stripes and dots
metadata.bookend_exempt_reason: lecture skill: opens on the narrated identity card then the hesitant writer; no composer cold open.

beats.narration_text: Patterns and Pixelation. Learn the two small functions that cut a shape into cells, and use them to pixelate an image and to draw checkerboards, stripes and dots.

beats.narration_text: Hallo. This is Liam, in for Bear. Most people think a checkerboard, a stripe or a grid of dots needs a pattern image. It does not. A pattern is math on the address, and the graphics card runs it for every pixel.

beats.narration_text: Six terms. A shader is a small program the graphics card runs to decide how something is drawn. U V is a point's address on the shape: zero to one across, zero to one down. A texture is an image a shader can read. A uniform is a value your game sets from outside. A cell is one square of a grid. A remainder is what is left after dividing.

terms.meaning: a small program the graphics card runs to decide how something is drawn
a point's address on the shape: 0 to 1 across, 0 to 1 down
an image a shader can read by address
a value your game sets from outside; every pixel sees the same one

beats.act: I · Which Cell, and Where in It
beats.narration_text: Chunky pixel blocks. A checkerboard. Moving stripes. A grid of dots. Four effects, and none of them needs a pattern image. All four come from one trick: cut the address into cells.

shot.visual_intent: Act title 'Which Cell, and Where in It' (serif 40) top-left. One-word labels land beside each panel as the voice names it.

beats.act: I · Which Cell, and Where in It
beats.narration_text: Start with the address. Across a shape it runs from zero to one. Multiply it by four and the address is stretched: it runs from zero to four. Each whole number it passes starts a new cell.

shot.visual_intent: The series ramp strip across the stage (a bar of light-to-mid greys, never near-black), end labels 0 and 1, caption 'UV.x' above it. It stretches: the right end label counts 1, 2, 3, 4 and the caption becomes 'UV.x × 4'; vertical tick lines grow at 1, 2 and 3, cutting the bar into four spans, and the whole numbers 0, 1, 2, 3 appear under the left end of each span. Midpoint still (45 to 55 %): the strip is stretched and labelled 0 to 4, caption 'UV.x × 4'; the ticks have not appeared yet.

right label counts to 4; caption becomes UV.x × 4

shot.motion_claim: The right label counts up to 4 while the ticks grow at each whole number.

beats.act: I · Which Cell, and Where in It
beats.narration_text: Floor tells you which cell you are in. Floor rounds down: zero point seven becomes zero, two point nine becomes two. So floor of the stretched address is the cell number: zero, one, two or three.

shot.visual_intent: The same ramp, now 0 to 4 with ticks at 1, 2, 3 (cast continues). A terracotta dot rides it with a live value above it; at the right a large readout 'floor = 0' (monospace) steps up only when the dot crosses a tick. The dot pauses at 0.7 (readout shows 0.7 and 0), runs on, pauses at 2.9 (readout shows 2.9 and 2). The span under the dot is underlined by a terracotta bar. Label under the bar: 'floor: rounds down'. Midpoint still (45 to 55 %): the dot is settled at 2.9 with the readout 'floor = 2' (it runs there between 36 and 44 %); the label 'floor: rounds down' is on screen.

beats.act: I · Which Cell, and Where in It
beats.narration_text: Fract keeps what floor throws away: the part after the point. Two point nine leaves point nine. Inside every cell it climbs from zero to one, then starts over.

shot.visual_intent: Axes on the cream stage: x from 0 to 4 along the bottom with ticks at the whole numbers, y from 0 to 1. A terracotta dot travels along x and draws the sawtooth of fract(x) behind it: a ramp from 0 to 1 that drops back to 0 at each whole number. At x = 2.9 the dot pauses at height 0.9 with the label 'fract(2.9) = 0.9'. The formula 'fract(x) = x − floor(x)' sits above the plot. Midpoint still (45 to 55 %): the dot is paused at 2.9, height 0.9, with the label 'fract(2.9) = 0.9'; the curve is drawn as far as 2.9.

beats.act: I · Which Cell, and Where in It
beats.narration_text: Together they pin down a spot exactly. Floor says which cell: column two, row one. Fract says where inside it: three tenths across, seven tenths down. That is the whole idea.

beats.act: I · Which Cell, and Where in It
beats.narration_text: Here is the map for the rest of the film. Floor gives one value per cell: that is pixelation and checkerboards. Fract gives a shape that repeats: that is stripes and dots. Use both, and you get a screen of dots.

beats.narration_text: To pixelate is to show a picture as big blocks. Inside a block, every pixel has the same color. So how does a shader pick one color for a whole block?

shot.visual_intent: Act title 'Pixelate Without the Drift' (serif 40) top-left. A real Godot render: the teal test sprite, smooth at first, then coarser in five steps until it is a chunky grid of blocks. Caption: 'pixelate: show a picture as big blocks'.

beats.narration_text: Make every pixel in a cell look up the picture at the same spot. One cell, one spot, one color. That is all pixelating is. The only question is which spot.

beats.narration_text: Walk one pixel through it. Address point six, four blocks. Times four is two point four. Floor gives two. Add a half: two and a half. Divide by four: point six two five, the middle of the third cell.

shot.visual_intent: A number line from 0 to 1 cut into four cells (ticks at 0.25, 0.5, 0.75). A terracotta marker sits at the address 0.6. Beside it an arithmetic stack types in line by line (monospace): '0.6 × 4 = 2.4', 'floor gives 2' (a word, never an arrow glyph), '+ 0.5 = 2.5', '÷ 4 = 0.625'. The third cell (0.5 to 0.75) gets a heavy outline and a terracotta lookup dot lands at its middle, 0.625. Midpoint still (45 to 55 %): the stack shows '0.6 × 4 = 2.4' and 'floor gives 2'; the marker is at 0.6; the '+ 0.5' line has not typed yet.
